meta.subject: science
meta.title: Acids, Bases & Salts
meta.summary: Where acids and bases are found, what water does to them, bases vs alkalis, indicators and neutralisation.

chunks.title: Sour or bitter?
body: Lemons, curd and vinegar taste **sour**: they contain **acids**.
Soap and wood ash feel **slippery** and taste **bitter**: they are **bases**.
Never taste lab chemicals! Scientists use **indicators** instead.

chunks.title: Acids vs bases
rows: Soap, wood ash, slaked lime, baking soda

chunks.title: Kitchen sort: acid or base?
chunks.intro: Sort each thing from home into the right jar. Its acid's name appears when you get it right!

challenges.text: **Mission:** sort all 8 things into Acid or Base.
challenges.explain: Sour things are acids. Bitter or soapy things are bases.

options.why: Citric acid is in lemons and oranges.
Acetic acid is in vinegar.
Formic acid is in an ant sting.

question.explanation: Curd is sour because of **lactic acid**.

chunks.title: Indicators
body: An **indicator** is a dye that changes colour in an acid or a base.
**Litmus**, **methyl orange** and **phenolphthalein** are lab indicators.
**Turmeric** and **China rose** (hibiscus) are natural indicators from home.

chunks.title: Lab · Dropper & Colour Detective
intro: Pick an indicator, then tap a tube to test it.
Then switch on **Mystery mode** and play detective!

challenges.text: **Mission:** in Mystery mode, find a tube that turns phenolphthalein **pink** and red litmus **blue**.
challenges.explain: Only a base turns phenolphthalein pink and red litmus blue.

challenges.text: Test all **six** tubes with at least one indicator.

question.prompt: A solution turns **phenolphthalein pink**. What kind of solution is it?

options.why: Acids keep phenolphthalein **colourless**.
Neutral solutions like pure water keep it colourless too.
You can! Phenolphthalein turns pink **only** in a base.

question.explanation: Phenolphthalein: colourless in acids and neutral solutions, **pink in bases**.

chunks.title: Why water matters
body: A dry acid can't change litmus. It needs **water** to wake up!
In water, an acid releases **hydrogen ions**, $\text{H}^+$.
In water, a base releases **hydroxide ions**, $\text{OH}^-$.

chunks.title: Lab · The Water Activation Microscope
chunks.intro: Follow the 3 steps. Watch the particle lens, the litmus strip and the bulb!

challenges.text: **Mission:** wake up the acid with water, then dissolve the base.
challenges.explain: Water splits acids into $\text{H}^+$ ions and bases into $\text{OH}^-$ ions. Free ions change litmus and carry electricity.

challenges.text: **Bonus:** do the splash test the **safe** way.

chunks.title: Safety rule
body: Always add **acid to water**, slowly. Never water to acid!
Mixing makes heat. Too much heat at once can make it splash.

chunks.title: Base or alkali?
body: A **base** is anything that can neutralise an acid.
An **alkali** is a base that **dissolves in water**.
So every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali.

chunks.title: Lab · The Dissolve Test
chunks.intro: Drop each base into the water and stir. Does it dissolve, or sink?

challenges.text: **Mission:** test all 4 bases and find the 2 that are **alkalis**.
challenges.explain: NaOH and KOH dissolve, so they are alkalis. Copper oxide and rust sink: they are bases, but not alkalis.

chunks.title: Game · The Egg-Yolk Sorter
chunks.intro: The white is **all bases**. The yolk is **alkalis**. Where does each one belong?

challenges.text: **Mission:** place all 5 bases in the right ring.
challenges.explain: All alkalis live inside the base family, because an alkali is just a base that dissolves in water!

question.prompt: Copper oxide neutralises acids but does **not** dissolve in water. It is…

options.text: A base, but not an alkali

options.why: An alkali must **dissolve in water**. Copper oxide sinks.
It neutralises acids, so it's a base, not an acid.

options.text: Neither a base nor an alkali
options.why: It neutralises acids, so it **is** a base.

question.explanation: It's a base (it neutralises acids) but not an alkali (it doesn't dissolve).

chunks.title: Neutralisation
body: When an acid and a base mix, they cancel each other out. This is **neutralisation**.
$$\text{Acid} + \text{Base} \rightarrow \text{Salt} + \text{Water}$$
A little heat is given out too.

chunks.title: Mini-game · Real-life cures
chunks.intro: Neutralisation fixes everyday problems. Pick the right remedy for each one.

challenges.explain: Each problem was an acid, so a mild base neutralised it.

chunks.title: Neutralisation in daily life
body: - **Indigestion**: an antacid (a mild base) cancels extra stomach acid.
- **Ant or bee sting**: baking soda (a base) soothes the acid.
- **Acidic soil**: farmers add lime (a base).
- **Factory waste**: acids are neutralised before they reach rivers.

mistakes.why: The acid and base are used up. They make a salt and **water**.
Neutralisation doesn't make a gas. It makes a salt and **water**.

questions.prompt: Curd tastes sour. Which acid does it contain?

options.why: Citric acid is in lemons and oranges, not curd.
Formic acid is in ant stings.
Acetic acid is in vinegar.

hints: Think about milk turning into curd.
The acid's name comes from the Latin word for milk, *lac*.

questions.prompt: An ant sting hurts because it injects ___ acid.

mistakes.why: Citric acid is in lemons. Ants inject **formic** acid.
Lactic acid is in curd. Ants inject **formic** acid.
Acetic acid is in vinegar. Ants inject **formic** acid.

hints: Its name comes from the Latin word for ant, *formica*.
questions.explanation: Ant stings contain **formic acid**, so a mild base like baking soda soothes them.

questions.prompt: What does an acid release when it dissolves in water?

options.why: $\text{OH}^-$ ions come from **bases** in water.
A dry acid can't even change litmus. It needs water to release its ions.
Salt forms when an acid **neutralises** a base, not when it dissolves.

hints: Remember the microscope lab: what popped out of the acid?
Acids → H… ions. Bases → OH… ions.

options.text: All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis

options.why: Bases like copper oxide don't dissolve in water, so they aren't alkalis.
Alkalis are a **kind of** base: the ones that dissolve in water.

options.text: An alkali is an acid that dissolves in water
options.why: An alkali is a **base** that dissolves in water.

hints: Think of the egg: which part is inside which?
An alkali is a base **plus** one extra thing: it dissolves in water.
So alkalis are a smaller group **inside** bases.
questions.explanation: An alkali is a water-soluble base, so all alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis.

questions.prompt: You add phenolphthalein to a clear solution and it **stays colourless**. What can you say?

options.why: Careful! Phenolphthalein is also colourless in **neutral** solutions like pure water. Use litmus to tell them apart.
A base would turn phenolphthalein **pink**.
It could be water, but an acid also keeps phenolphthalein colourless.

hints: Which kind of solution turns phenolphthalein pink?
Only bases turn it pink. So if it stays colourless, it isn't a base.
Not a base → it's an **acid or neutral**. Phenolphthalein alone can't tell which.
questions.explanation: Colourless phenolphthalein rules out a base, but can't separate acid from neutral.

questions.prompt: What do you get when an acid **neutralises** a base?

options.why: The acid is used up in neutralisation.
Neutralisation doesn't make a gas.
New substances form: a salt and water.

hints: Neutralisation is a chemical change, so something new forms.

items.title: In water
body: Acid → releases $\text{H}^+$ (hydrogen ions)
Base → releases $\text{OH}^-$ (hydroxide ions)
Safety: add **acid to water**, never water to acid.

items.title: Base vs alkali
body: **Alkali** = a base that dissolves in water (NaOH, KOH).
Copper oxide, rust: bases, **not** alkalis.
All alkalis are bases; not all bases are alkalis.
